claim: Several areas of the world suffer a notably high incidence of Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli, including Scotland, Ireland, Argentina, and the Canadian province of Alberta.
source: Several areas around the globe experience exceptionally high incidence of Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (STEC), including the virulent serotype E. coli O157:H7. These include Scotland, (Innocent et al., 2005) Ireland, (Óhaiseadha et al., 2017) Argentina, (Rivero et al., 2010) and the Canadian province of Alberta (Lisboa et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature for each region mentioned.

claim: All high-incidence STEC regions are home to large populations of agricultural ruminants, STEC's primary reservoir.
source: All are home to large populations of agricultural ruminants, STEC's primary reservoir.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about STEC reservoirs and is stated as a general observation about the high-incidence regions.

claim: There are many regions with similar ruminant populations where STEC incidence is unremarkable.
source: However, there are many regions with similar ruminant populations where STEC incidence is unremarkable.
evidence: This is stated as a contrasting observation to highlight that ruminant populations alone do not explain high incidence.

claim: What differentiates high-risk STEC regions is unclear.
source: What differentiates high-risk regions is unclear.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the current state of knowledge regarding high-risk regions.

claim: Systematic STEC surveillance is only conducted in limited parts of the world.
source: Moreover, with systematic STEC surveillance only conducted in limited parts of the world, (Kirk et al., 2015) there may be unidentified regions with exceptionally high disease burden.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kirk et al., 2015.

claim: There may be unidentified regions with exceptionally high STEC disease burden.
source: Moreover, with systematic STEC surveillance only conducted in limited parts of the world, (Kirk et al., 2015) there may be unidentified regions with exceptionally high disease burden.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the limited surveillance mentioned.

claim: STEC infections can arise from local reservoirs, transmitted through food, water, direct animal contact, or contact with contaminated environmental matrices.
source: STEC infections can arise from local reservoirs, transmitted through food, water, direct animal contact, or contact with contaminated environmental matrices.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about STEC transmission routes.

claim: The most common STEC reservoirs include domesticated ruminants such as cattle, sheep, and goats.
source: The most common reservoirs include domesticated ruminants such as cattle, sheep, and goats.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about STEC reservoirs.

claim: Animal contact and consumption of contaminated meat and dairy products are significant risk factors for STEC.
source: Animal contact and consumption of contaminated meat and dairy products are significant risk factors for STEC, as are consumption of leafy greens, tomatoes, and herbs and recreational swimming that have been contaminated by feces from domestic ruminants (FAO/WHO, 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to FAO/WHO, 2018.

claim: Consumption of leafy greens, tomatoes, and herbs contaminated by feces from domestic ruminants are significant risk factors for STEC.
source: Animal contact and consumption of contaminated meat and dairy products are significant risk factors for STEC, as are consumption of leafy greens, tomatoes, and herbs and recreational swimming that have been contaminated by feces from domestic ruminants (FAO/WHO, 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to FAO/WHO, 2018.

claim: Recreational swimming in water contaminated by feces from domestic ruminants is a significant risk factor for STEC.
source: Animal contact and consumption of contaminated meat and dairy products are significant risk factors for STEC, as are consumption of leafy greens, tomatoes, and herbs and recreational swimming that have been contaminated by feces from domestic ruminants (FAO/WHO, 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to FAO/WHO, 2018.

claim: STEC has been isolated from a variety of animal species including deer and swine.
source: While STEC has been isolated from a variety of other animal species and outbreaks have been linked to species such as deer (Laidler et al., 2013) and swine, (Honish et al., 2014) it is unclear what roles they play as maintenance or intermediate hosts.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Laidler et al., 2013 and Honish et al., 2014.

claim: Outbreaks of STEC have been linked to deer and swine.
source: While STEC has been isolated from a variety of other animal species and outbreaks have been linked to species such as deer (Laidler et al., 2013) and swine, (Honish et al., 2014) it is unclear what roles they play as maintenance or intermediate hosts.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Laidler et al., 2013 and Honish et al., 2014.

claim: It is unclear what roles species such as deer and swine play as maintenance or intermediate hosts for STEC.
source: While STEC has been isolated from a variety of other animal species and outbreaks have been linked to species such as deer (Laidler et al., 2013) and swine, (Honish et al., 2014) it is unclear what roles they play as maintenance or intermediate hosts.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the current state of knowledge regarding these species as STEC hosts.

claim: STEC infections can be imported through food items traded nationally and internationally.
source: STEC infections can be imported through food items traded nationally and internationally, as has been seen with E. coli O157:H7 outbreaks in romaine lettuce from the United States (Bottichio et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bottichio et al., 2020 as an example.

claim: E. coli O157:H7 outbreaks have been linked to romaine lettuce from the United States.
source: STEC infections can be imported through food items traded nationally and internationally, as has been seen with E. coli O157:H7 outbreaks in romaine lettuce from the United States (Bottichio et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bottichio et al., 2020.

claim: Secondary transmission is believed to cause approximately 15% of STEC cases.
source: Secondary transmission is believed to cause approximately 15% of cases, but transmission of the pathogen is not believed to be sustained through person-to-person transmission over the long term (Tack et al., 2021; Kintz et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tack et al., 2021 and Kintz et al., 2017.

claim: Transmission of STEC is not believed to be sustained through person-to-person transmission over the long term.
source: Secondary transmission is believed to cause approximately 15% of cases, but transmission of the pathogen is not believed to be sustained through person-to-person transmission over the long term (Tack et al., 2021; Kintz et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tack et al., 2021 and Kintz et al., 2017.

claim: Living near cattle and other domesticated ruminants has been linked to STEC incidence, particularly for E. coli O157:H7.
source: Living near cattle and other domesticated ruminants has been linked to STEC incidence, particularly for E. coli O157:H7 (Óhaiseadha et al., 2017; Jaros et al., 2013; Elson et al., 2018; Frank et al., 2008; Friesema et al., 2011; Mulder et al., 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Studies suggest an important role for local reservoirs in STEC epidemiology.
source: These studies suggest an important role for local reservoirs in STEC epidemiology.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited studies about proximity to ruminants.

claim: Across the 1215 isolates included in the analyses, 12,273 core genome SNPs were identified.
source: Across the 1215 isolates included in the analyses, we identified 12,273 core genome SNPs.
evidence: This is a direct report of data from the genomic analysis.

claim: Clade G(vi) constituted 73.6% (n=894) of all isolates.
source: Clade G(vi) constituted 73.6% (n=894) of all isolates (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is a direct report of data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Clade A included non-Alberta isolates, two human isolates from Alberta, and no Alberta cattle isolates.
source: Clade A, which is the most distinct of the E. coli O157:H7 clades, included non-Alberta isolates, two human isolates from Alberta, and no Alberta cattle isolates.
evidence: This is a direct report of data from the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The majority of all Alberta isolates belonged to the G(vi) clade (582 of 659; 88.3%).
source: The majority of all Alberta isolates belonged to the G(vi) clade (582 of 659; 88.3%), compared to 281 of the 1560 (18.0%) randomly sampled U.S. PulseNet isolates that were successfully assembled and QCed.
evidence: This is a direct report of data from the analysis.

claim: 281 of 1560 (18.0%) randomly sampled U.S. PulseNet isolates belonged to the G(vi) clade.
source: The majority of all Alberta isolates belonged to the G(vi) clade (582 of 659; 88.3%), compared to 281 of the 1560 (18.0%) randomly sampled U.S. PulseNet isolates that were successfully assembled and QCed.
evidence: This is a direct report of data from the analysis.

claim: Among the 62 non-randomly sampled global isolates, only 2 (3.2%) were clade G(vi).
source: Among the 62 non-randomly sampled global isolates, only 2 (3.2%) were clade G(vi) (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a direct report of data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: There were 682 (76.3%) clade G(vi) isolates with the stx1a/stx2a profile.
source: There were 682 (76.3%) clade G(vi) isolates with the stx1a/stx2a profile and 210 (23.5%) with the stx2a-only profile, compared to 2 (0.6%) and 58 (18.1%), respectively, among the 321 isolates outside the G(vi) clade (Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct report of data shown in Table 1.

claim: There were 210 (23.5%) clade G(vi) isolates with the stx2a-only profile.
source: There were 682 (76.3%) clade G(vi) isolates with the stx1a/stx2a profile and 210 (23.5%) with the stx2a-only profile, compared to 2 (0.6%) and 58 (18.1%), respectively, among the 321 isolates outside the G(vi) clade (Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct report of data shown in Table 1.

claim: Among the 321 isolates outside the G(vi) clade, 2 (0.6%) had the stx1a/stx2a profile and 58 (18.1%) had the stx2a-only profile.
source: There were 682 (76.3%) clade G(vi) isolates with the stx1a/stx2a profile and 210 (23.5%) with the stx2a-only profile, compared to 2 (0.6%) and 58 (18.1%), respectively, among the 321 isolates outside the G(vi) clade (Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct report of data shown in Table 1.

claim: Among sampled human cases, 19 (15.7%; 95% CI 9.7%, 23.4%) were within five SNPs of a sampled cattle strain.
source: Among sampled human cases, 19 (15.7%; 95% CI 9.7%, 23.4%) were within five SNPs of a sampled cattle strain.
evidence: This is a direct report of data from the SNP distance analysis.

claim: The median SNP distance between cattle sequences was 45 (IQR 36–56).
source: The median SNP distance between cattle sequences was 45 (IQR 36–56), compared to 54 (IQR 43–229) SNPs between human sequences from cases in Alberta during the same years.
evidence: This is a direct report of data from the SNP distance analysis.

claim: The median SNP distance between human sequences from cases in Alberta was 54 (IQR 43–229).
source: The median SNP distance between cattle sequences was 45 (IQR 36–56), compared to 54 (IQR 43–229) SNPs between human sequences from cases in Alberta during the same years.
evidence: This is a direct report of data from the SNP distance analysis.

claim: The phylogeny generated by the primary structured coalescent analysis indicated cattle were the primary reservoir.
source: The phylogeny generated by our primary structured coalescent analysis indicated cattle were the primary reservoir, with a high probability that the hosts at nodes along the backbone of the tree were cattle (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a direct interpretation of the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The root of the phylogeny was estimated at 1802 (95% HPD 1731, 1861).
source: The root was estimated at 1802 (95% HPD 1731, 1861).
evidence: This is a direct report of data from the phylodynamic analysis.

claim: The most recent common ancestor (MRCA) of clade G(vi) strains in Alberta was inferred to be a cattle strain, dated to 1969 (95% HPD 1959, 1979).
source: The most recent common ancestor (MRCA) of clade G(vi) strains in Alberta was inferred to be a cattle strain, dated to 1969 (95% HPD 1959, 1979).
evidence: This is a direct report of data from the phylodynamic analysis.

claim: The mean clock rate for the core genome was estimated at 9.65×10–5 (95% HPD 8.13×10–5, 1.13×10–4) substitutions/site/year.
source: With our assumption of a relaxed molecular clock, the mean clock rate for the core genome was estimated at 9.65×10–5 (95% HPD 8.13×10–5, 1.13×10–4) substitutions/site/year.
evidence: This is a direct report of data from the phylodynamic analysis.

claim: The effective population size, Ne, of the human E. coli O157:H7 population was estimated as 1060 (95% HPD 698, 1477).
source: The effective population size, Ne, of the human E. coli O157:H7 population, was estimated as 1060 (95% HPD 698, 1477), and for cattle as 73 (95% HPD 50, 98).
evidence: This is a direct report of data from the phylodynamic analysis.

claim: The effective population size, Ne, for cattle was estimated as 73 (95% HPD 50, 98).
source: The effective population size, Ne, of the human E. coli O157:H7 population, was estimated as 1060 (95% HPD 698, 1477), and for cattle as 73 (95% HPD 50, 98).
evidence: This is a direct report of data from the phylodynamic analysis.

claim: 108 (95% HPD 104, 112) human lineages arose from cattle lineages.
source: We estimated 108 (95% HPD 104, 112) human lineages arose from cattle lineages, and 14 (95% HPD 5, 23) arose from other human lineages (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a direct report of data from the phylodynamic analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: 14 (95% HPD 5, 23) human lineages arose from other human lineages.
source: We estimated 108 (95% HPD 104, 112) human lineages arose from cattle lineages, and 14 (95% HPD 5, 23) arose from other human lineages (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a direct report of data from the phylodynamic analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: 88.5% of human lineages seen in Alberta from 2007 to 2015 arose from cattle lineages.
source: In other words, 88.5% of human lineages seen in Alberta from 2007 to 2015 arose from cattle lineages.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the state transition data from the phylodynamic analysis.

claim: The sensitivity analysis of equal numbers of isolates from cattle and humans estimated that 94.3% of human lineages arose from cattle lineages.
source: Our sensitivity analysis of equal numbers of isolates from cattle and humans was largely consistent with our primary results, estimating that 94.3% of human lineages arose from cattle lineages (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a direct report of data from the sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: 11 locally persistent lineages (LPLs) were identified in the primary analysis.
source: In our primary analysis, we identified 11 locally persistent lineages (LPLs) (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a direct report of findings from the analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: LPLs included a range of 5 to 26 isolates, with an average of 10.
source: After reincorporating down-sampled isolates, LPLs included a range of 5 (G(vi)-AB LPL 9)–26 isolates (G(vi)-AB LPL 1), with an average of 10.
evidence: This is a direct report of data from the LPL analysis.

claim: LPLs persisted for 5–9 years, with the average LPL spanning 8 years.
source: LPLs persisted for 5–9 y, with the average LPL spanning 8 y.
evidence: This is a direct report of data from the LPL analysis.

claim: All LPL MRCAs had posterior probabilities of 99.7–100%.
source: By definition, MRCAs of each LPL were required to have a posterior probability ≥95% on the MCC tree, and in practice, all had posterior probabilities of 99.7–100%.
evidence: This is a direct report of data from the phylodynamic analysis.

claim: The sensitivity analysis of equal numbers of isolates from cattle and humans identified 10 of the same 11 LPLs.
source: Our sensitivity analysis of equal numbers of isolates from cattle and humans identified 10 of the same 11 LPLs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a direct report of findings from the sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: G(vi)-AB LPLs 1–4, 6–8, and 9 and 10 were clustered with MRCAs inferred in 1996 (95% HPD 1992, 1999), 1998 (95% HPD 1995, 2000), and 1993 (95% HPD 1989, 1996), respectively.
source: LPLs tended to be clustered on the MCC tree. G(vi)-AB LPLs 1–4, 6–8, and 9 and 10 were clustered with MRCAs inferred in 1996 (95% HPD 1992, 1999), 1998 (95% HPD 1995, 2000), and 1993 (95% HPD 1989, 1996), respectively (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a direct report of data from the phylodynamic analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Cattle were the inferred host of all three ancestral nodes of the LPL clusters.
source: Cattle were the inferred host of all three ancestral nodes.
evidence: This is a direct report of findings from the phylodynamic analysis.

claim: LPLs included 71 of 108 (65.7%; 95% CI 56.0%, 74.6%) cattle isolates.
source: LPLs included 71 of 108 (65.7%; 95% CI 56.0%, 74.6%) cattle and 46 of 121 (38.0%; 95% CI 29.3%, 47.3%) human isolates.
evidence: This is a direct report of data from the LPL analysis.

claim: LPLs included 46 of 121 (38.0%; 95% CI 29.3%, 47.3%) human isolates.
source: LPLs included 71 of 108 (65.7%; 95% CI 56.0%, 74.6%) cattle and 46 of 121 (38.0%; 95% CI 29.3%, 47.3%) human isolates.
evidence: This is a direct report of data from the LPL analysis.

claim: Of the remaining human isolates, 33 (27.3%) were associated with imported infections and 42 (34.7%) with infections from transient local strains.
source: Of the remaining human isolates, 33 (27.3%) were associated with imported infections and 42 (34.7%) with infections from transient local strains.
evidence: This is a direct report of data from the analysis of non-LPL isolates.

claim: Of the remaining cattle isolates, 11 (10.2%) were imported and 26 (24.1%) were associated with transmission from transient strains.
source: Of the remaining cattle isolates, 11 (10.2%) were imported and 26 (24.1%) were associated with transmission from transient strains.
evidence: This is a direct report of data from the analysis of non-LPL isolates.

claim: Of the 117 isolates in LPLs, 7 (6.0%) carried only stx2a, and the rest stx1a/stx2a.
source: Of the 117 isolates in LPLs, 7 (6.0%) carried only stx2a, and the rest stx1a/stx2a.
evidence: This is a direct report of data from the stx profile analysis.

claim: Among the 112 non-LPL isolates, 1 (0.9%) was stx1a-only, 27 (24.1%) were stx2a-only, 5 (4.5%) were stx2c-only, 68 (60.7%) were stx1a/stx2a, 6 (5.4%) were stx1a/stx2c, and 5 (4.5%) were stx2a/stx2c.
source: Among the 112 non-LPL isolates, 1 (0.9%) was stx1a-only, 27 (24.1%) were stx2a-only, 5 (4.5%) were stx2c-only, 68 (60.7%) were stx1a/stx2a, 6 (5.4%) were stx1a/stx2c, and 5 (4.5%) were stx2a/stx2c.
evidence: This is a direct report of data from the stx profile analysis.

claim: Six of the 11 LPLs identified in the primary analysis (G(vi)-AB LPLs 1, 2, 4, 7, 10, and 11) continued to cause disease during the 2016–2019 period.
source: To understand long-term persistence, we expanded the phylogeny with additional Alberta Health isolates from 2009 to 2019. Six of the 11 LPLs identified in our primary analysis, G(vi)-AB LPLs 1, 2, 4, 7, 10, and 11, continued to cause disease during the 2016–2019 period (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a direct report of findings from the extended analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Of 217 sequenced cases reported during 2018 and 2019, 162 (74.7%; 95% CI 68.3%, 80.3%) arose from Alberta LPLs.
source: Of 217 sequenced cases reported during these 2 y, 162 (74.7%; 95% CI 68.3%, 80.3%) arose from Alberta LPLs.
evidence: This is a direct report of data from the extended analysis.

claim: 83 (51.2%; 95% CI 43.3%, 59.2%) of the LPL isolates from 2018-2019 encoded only stx2a and the rest stx1a/stx2a.
source: The stx profile of LPL isolates shifted as compared to the primary analysis, with 83 (51.2%; 95% CI 43.3%, 59.2%) of the LPL isolates encoding only stx2a and the rest stx1a/stx2a (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a direct report of data from the extended analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Among the 55 non-LPL isolates during 2018–2019, 16 (29.1%; 95% CI 17.6%, 42.9%) were stx2c-only.
source: Among the 55 non-LPL isolates during 2018–2019, the stx2c-only profile emerged with 16 (29.1%; 95% CI 17.6%, 42.9%) isolates, stx2a-only was found in six (10.9%; 95% CI 4.1%, 22.2%) isolates, and five (9.1%; 95% CI 3.0%, 20.0%) isolates carried both stx2a and stx2c.
evidence: This is a direct report of data from the extended analysis.

claim: Among the 55 non-LPL isolates during 2018–2019, 6 (10.9%; 95% CI 4.1%, 22.2%) were stx2a-only.
source: Among the 55 non-LPL isolates during 2018–2019, the stx2c-only profile emerged with 16 (29.1%; 95% CI 17.6%, 42.9%) isolates, stx2a-only was found in six (10.9%; 95% CI 4.1%, 22.2%) isolates, and five (9.1%; 95% CI 3.0%, 20.0%) isolates carried both stx2a and stx2c.
evidence: This is a direct report of data from the extended analysis.

claim: Among the 55 non-LPL isolates during 2018–2019, 5 (9.1%; 95% CI 3.0%, 20.0%) carried both stx2a and stx2c.
source: Among the 55 non-LPL isolates during 2018–2019, the stx2c-only profile emerged with 16 (29.1%; 95% CI 17.6%, 42.9%) isolates, stx2a-only was found in six (10.9%; 95% CI 4.1%, 22.2%) isolates, and five (9.1%; 95% CI 3.0%, 20.0%) isolates carried both stx2a and stx2c.
evidence: This is a direct report of data from the extended analysis.

claim: All five large (≥10 cases) sequenced outbreaks in Alberta during the study period were within clade G(vi).
source: All five large (≥10 cases) sequenced outbreaks in Alberta during the study period were within clade G(vi).
evidence: This is a direct report of findings from the outbreak analysis.

claim: G(vi)-AB LPLs 2 and 7 gave rise to three large outbreaks, accounting for 117 cases (both sequenced and unsequenced).
source: G(vi)-AB LPLs 2 and 7 gave rise to three large outbreaks, accounting for 117 cases (both sequenced and unsequenced), including 83 from an extended outbreak by a single strain in 2018 and 2019, defined as isolates within five SNPs of one another.
evidence: This is a direct report of findings from the outbreak analysis.

claim: An extended outbreak by a single strain in 2018 and 2019 accounted for 83 cases.
source: G(vi)-AB LPLs 2 and 7 gave rise to three large outbreaks, accounting for 117 cases (both sequenced and unsequenced), including 83 from an extended outbreak by a single strain in 2018 and 2019, defined as isolates within five SNPs of one another.
evidence: This is a direct report of findings from the outbreak analysis.

claim: The two large outbreaks that did not arise from LPLs both occurred in 2014 and were responsible for 164 cases.
source: The two large outbreaks that did not arise from LPLs both occurred in 2014 and were responsible for 164 cases.
evidence: This is a direct report of findings from the outbreak analysis.

claim: Of the 494 U.S. isolates analyzed, nine (1.8%; 95% CI 0.8%, 3.4%) occurred within Alberta LPLs after re-incorporating down-sampled isolates.
source: Of the 494 U.S. isolates analyzed, nine (1.8%; 95% CI 0.8%, 3.4%) occurred within Alberta LPLs after re-incorporating down-sampled isolates (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a direct report of data from the global analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: None of the 62 global isolates were associated with Alberta LPLs.
source: None of the 62 global isolates were associated with Alberta LPLs.
evidence: This is a direct report of data from the global analysis.

claim: The 9 U.S. isolates within Alberta LPLs were part of G(vi)-AB LPLs 2 (n=3), 4 (n=4), 7 (n=1), and 11 (n=1).
source: The 9 U.S. isolates were part of G(vi)-AB LPLs 2 (n=3), 4 (n=4), 7 (n=1), and 11 (n=1), all of which had Alberta isolates that spanned 9–13 y and predated the U.S. isolates.
evidence: This is a direct report of data from the global analysis.

claim: All LPLs with U.S. isolates had Alberta isolates that spanned 9–13 years and predated the U.S. isolates.
source: The 9 U.S. isolates were part of G(vi)-AB LPLs 2 (n=3), 4 (n=4), 7 (n=1), and 11 (n=1), all of which had Alberta isolates that spanned 9–13 y and predated the U.S. isolates.
evidence: This is a direct report of data from the global analysis.

claim: There was no evidence of U.S. or global ancestors of LPLs.
source: There was no evidence of U.S. or global ancestors of LPLs.
evidence: This is a direct statement of findings from the global analysis.

claim: 11.0% of combined human and cattle Alberta lineages were imported based on migration events calculated from the structured tree.
source: Based on migration events calculated from the structured tree, we estimated that 11.0% of combined human and cattle Alberta lineages were imported (Table 2).
evidence: This is a direct report of data from the structured coalescent analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: Alberta sequences were separated from U.S. sequences by a median of 63 (IQR 45–236) SNPs.
source: Alberta sequences were separated from U.S. and global sequences by a median of 63 (IQR 45–236) and 225 (IQR 209–249) SNPs, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct report of data from the SNP distance analysis.

claim: Alberta sequences were separated from global sequences by a median of 225 (IQR 209–249) SNPs.
source: Alberta sequences were separated from U.S. and global sequences by a median of 63 (IQR 45–236) and 225 (IQR 209–249) SNPs, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct report of data from the SNP distance analysis.

claim: Of the 217 Alberta human isolates from 2018 and 2019, 160 (73.7%) were still associated with LPLs after the addition of U.S. and global isolates.
source: Of the 217 Alberta human isolates from 2018 and 2019, 160 (73.7%) were still associated with LPLs after the addition of U.S. and global isolates, demonstrating the stability of the extended analysis results.
evidence: This is a direct report of data from the global analysis.

claim: The study provided quantitative estimates of cattle-to-human migration in a high-incidence region, the first such estimates of which the authors are aware.
source: Our study has provided quantitative estimates of cattle-to-human migration in a high-incidence region, the first such estimates of which we are aware.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the novelty of the study's findings.

claim: 88.5% of strains infecting humans arose from cattle lineages.
source: We showed that 88.5% of strains infecting humans arose from cattle lineages.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary finding from the phylodynamic analysis.

claim: The estimate of the origin of the E. coli O157:H7 serotype at 1802 (95% HPD 1731, 1861) was somewhat earlier than previous estimates.
source: Our estimate of the origin of the serotype, at 1802 (95% HPD 1731, 1861), was somewhat earlier than previous estimates, but consistent with global (1890; 95% HPD 1845, 1925) Franz et al., 2019 and the United Kingdom (1840; 95% HPD 1817, 1855) (Dallman et al., 2015) studies that used comparable methods.
evidence: This compares the study's estimate with previous estimates from cited studies.

claim: The dating of the G(vi) clade in Alberta to 1969 (95% HPD 1959, 1979) corresponds to proposed migrations of clade G into Canada from the U.S. in 1965–1977.
source: Our dating of the G(vi) clade in Alberta to 1969 (95% HPD 1959, 1979) also corresponds to proposed migrations of clade G into Canada from the U.S. in 1965–1977 (Franz et al., 2019).
evidence: This compares the study's estimate with previous findings from Franz et al., 2019.

claim: All 11 LPLs were in clade G(vi).
source: Further supporting the evolution of the LPLs within Alberta, all 11 LPLs were in clade G(vi), several were phylogenetically related with MRCAs dating to the late 1990 s, and few non-Alberta isolates fell within LPLs.
evidence: This is a direct report of findings from the LPL analysis.

claim: Several LPLs were phylogenetically related with MRCAs dating to the late 1990s.
source: Further supporting the evolution of the LPLs within Alberta, all 11 LPLs were in clade G(vi), several were phylogenetically related with MRCAs dating to the late 1990 s, and few non-Alberta isolates fell within LPLs.
evidence: This is a direct report of findings from the phylodynamic analysis.

claim: Few non-Alberta isolates fell within LPLs.
source: Further supporting the evolution of the LPLs within Alberta, all 11 LPLs were in clade G(vi), several were phylogenetically related with MRCAs dating to the late 1990 s, and few non-Alberta isolates fell within LPLs.
evidence: This is a direct report of findings from the global analysis.

claim: Based on the LPL analysis, 27% of human E. coli O157:H7 isolates were imported into Alberta.
source: Based on our LPL analysis, we estimated only 27% of human and 10% of cattle E. coli O157:H7 isolates were imported.
evidence: This is a direct report of the estimate from the LPL analysis.

claim: Based on the LPL analysis, 10% of cattle E. coli O157:H7 isolates were imported into Alberta.
source: Based on our LPL analysis, we estimated only 27% of human and 10% of cattle E. coli O157:H7 isolates were imported.
